stem: A company's web application stores its data in a Single-AZ Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The company wants to fix a performance problem without any change to the application's SQL queries. During spiky traffic, thousands of short-lived AWS Lambda invocations open connections, and the database returns too many connections errors at low CPU use. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: thousands of short-lived AWS Lambda invocations open connections
too many connections errors at low CPU use

options.text: Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance, and change the application's connection settings to use the proxy endpoint.
options.why: Lambda functions make [frequent short database connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-lambda-connection-pooling), and the proxy keeps a [smaller number of long-lived connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-candidate-too-many-connections) open to the database.

options.text: Create a read replica of the DB instance, and change the application's connection settings to send its read-only queries to the replica.
options.why: A replica takes reads, but each Lambda environment still opens its own connection, and high concurrency can [exhaust database connection limits](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vpc-db-connections-rds-proxy) again.
options.misconception: a second DB instance fixes a storm of short-lived connections

options.text: Move the database to PostgreSQL on Amazon EC2 instances, and run a connection pooler and streaming read replicas that the team manages.
options.why: A self-managed pooler works, but on EC2 the team owns [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) of the database.
options.misconception: builds connection pooling by hand when a managed proxy exists

options.text: Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, so that the standby instance also serves part of the query load.
options.why: The standby [doesn't serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), and a Multi-AZ deployment does not pool the connections of the functions.

explanation: The errors come from the number of connections, not from CPU. Lambda functions benefit from the [connection pooling offered by RDS Proxy](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-lambda-connection-pooling). With multiplexing, the proxy [keeps a smaller number of connections open](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-multiplexing-fewer-db-connections) to the DB instance, so the connection errors become less likely without a larger instance.
takeaway: Connection errors at low CPU point to RDS Proxy; heavy reads point to a read replica.
twin: If the stem said "Dashboard read queries keep the CPU use near 90 percent at peak, but the number of database connections stays low" instead: a read replica, because it serves [read-heavy database workloads](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-definition).
say: The database is out of connections, not CPU, so I'd put RDS Proxy in front to pool them.

stem: A company runs an order database on an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with General Purpose SSD storage. Twice last quarter, the allocated storage filled up, and the application could not write new orders until an engineer added storage. The data grows at an unpredictable rate. The company does not want to pay in advance for a large amount of storage that it does not use. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on free storage space that invokes an AWS Lambda function to increase the allocated storage.
options.why: It works, but the team builds and maintains the alarm and the function, which storage autoscaling does without any code.
options.misconception: builds storage scaling by hand when RDS has it built in

options.text: Allocate twice the current storage now, and reduce the allocated storage again after the company deletes old orders each year.
options.why: Allocated storage cannot shrink, because [you can't deallocate space](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-increase-min-10-percent), so the extra storage stays and the company pays for it.

options.text: Change the storage type to Provisioned IOPS SSD, so that busy write periods no longer fill the allocated storage.
options.why: Provisioned IOPS gives [low I/O latency and consistent I/O throughput](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-piops-for-production), not more space, so the storage still fills.
options.misconception: confuses storage performance (IOPS) with storage capacity

options.text: Turn on storage autoscaling for the DB instance, and set a maximum storage threshold that fits the company's budget.
options.why: When RDS detects low free space, [it automatically scales up your storage](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-autoscaling-unpredictable), and the [maximum storage threshold](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-autoscaling-max-threshold) caps the growth.

explanation: Storage autoscaling is the RDS feature for this case, and AWS points to it [if your workload is unpredictable](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-autoscaling-unpredictable). Turning it on [doesn't cause any downtime](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-autoscaling-no-downtime). Storage grows in steps as the data grows, so the company does not pay for a large reserve in advance, and the team does not watch the free space.
takeaway: Storage that fills at an unpredictable rate points to storage autoscaling with a maximum threshold.
twin: If the stem said "the database needs faster, more consistent storage, not more space" instead: Provisioned IOPS storage, because it gives [low I/O latency and consistent I/O throughput](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-piops-for-production).
say: I'd turn on storage autoscaling with a maximum threshold, so storage grows before it fills.

stem: An audit finds that a company's Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance was created without encryption. The company must encrypt the data at rest with an AWS KMS key, and the encryption must also cover the automated backups and any future read replicas. A short maintenance window for the cutover is acceptable. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: encrypt the data at rest with an AWS KMS key

options.text: Modify the DB instance to turn on encryption with the KMS key, and apply the change during the next maintenance window.
options.why: You can [only encrypt an Amazon RDS DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-only-at-create) when you create it, so a modification cannot turn encryption on.

options.text: Create a read replica of the DB instance that is encrypted with the KMS key, and promote the replica to a standalone DB instance.
options.why: For an encrypted read replica, [the source DB instance must be encrypted](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-encrypted-needs-encrypted-source), and this source is not encrypted.

options.text: Take a snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption under the KMS key, and restore a new DB instance from the encrypted copy.
options.why: RDS lets you [encrypt a copy of an unencrypted snapshot](../facts/rds.md#rds-encrypt-existing-via-snapshot-copy) and [restore an encrypted DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-encrypt-existing-via-snapshot-copy) from that copy, with a short cutover.

options.text: Create a new encrypted DB instance with the KMS key, and move the data with a dump and restore that the team scripts and runs.
options.why: It works, but the team writes, tests and runs the dump and the restore, which a snapshot copy does without scripts.
options.misconception: moves the data by hand when an encrypted snapshot copy does it

explanation: RDS encrypts a DB instance at creation, [not after the DB instance is created](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-only-at-create), so the fix is a new, encrypted DB instance. An encrypted snapshot copy creates it without scripts. After the restore, encryption covers the [logs, automated backups, read replicas, and snapshots](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-at-rest-scope). The application moves to the new endpoint in the maintenance window.
takeaway: To encrypt an existing DB instance, copy a snapshot with encryption and restore a new DB instance.
twin: If the stem said "a DB instance that the company will create next month" instead: turn on encryption at creation, because RDS encrypts a DB instance then and [not after the DB instance is created](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-only-at-create).
say: Encryption is set at creation, so I'd copy a snapshot with the KMS key and restore from it.

stem: A company is moving a legacy packaged application from its data center to AWS. The application uses a Microsoft SQL Server database. The software vendor supports the application only when the vendor's monitoring agent runs on the operating system of the database host. The company wants AWS to automate as much database administration as possible, such as backups and patching. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: agent runs on the operating system of the database host
automate as much database administration as possible

options.text: Run the database on Amazon RDS for SQL Server, and install the vendor's agent on the host of the DB instance.
options.why: Standard Amazon RDS [doesn't let you access the underlying host](../facts/rds.md#rds-custom-os-access), so the vendor's agent has no place to run.

options.text: Run SQL Server on Amazon EC2 instances that the team manages, and install the vendor's agent on each instance.
options.why: It works, but with SQL Server on EC2 the team owns [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks).
options.misconception: takes full control of the host when a managed option gives the access that is needed

options.text: Move the database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, and run the vendor's agent on an EC2 instance next to the cluster.
options.why: The packaged application is built for SQL Server, and an agent on a separate EC2 instance is not on the database host.
options.misconception: changes the engine of a packaged application and places the agent away from the database host

options.text: Run the database on Amazon RDS Custom for SQL Server, and install the vendor's agent on the DB instance host.
options.why: RDS Custom gives the agent access to the host, and AWS still automates most of the database administration for the team.

explanation: The vendor needs access to the operating system, and the company wants managed administration. RDS Custom automates database administration and lets you [customize your database environment and operating system](../facts/rds.md#rds-custom-os-access). AWS says that [Amazon RDS Custom is the better choice](../facts/rds.md#rds-custom-vs-rds-vs-ec2) when you need administrative rights to the database and the underlying operating system.
takeaway: Host access plus managed administration points to RDS Custom; full control points to EC2.
twin: If the stem said "The vendor supports the application on any managed SQL Server database" instead: Amazon RDS for SQL Server, because the agent is not needed and standard RDS leaves less administration to the team.
say: The vendor needs the host, so I'd use RDS Custom, which still automates most of the administration.

stem: A company created an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance for a project that has ended. The DB instance has automated backups with a backup retention period of 7 days. The company will delete the DB instance today to stop paying for it. A regulation requires the company to retain the current data for 2 years, so that the company can restore the data if an auditor asks. What should the company do when it deletes the DB instance?
keywords: retain the current data for 2 years

options.text: Create a final DB snapshot as part of the deletion, and keep the snapshot until the 2 years end.
options.why: [If you take a final snapshot](../facts/rds.md#rds-delete-final-snapshot-option), you can restore the deleted DB instance from it later.

options.text: Delete the DB instance without a final snapshot, because the automated backups stay available after the deletion.
options.why: Unless the company chooses to retain them, [all automated backups are deleted](../facts/rds.md#rds-delete-instance-automated-backups-deleted) with the DB instance.

options.text: Raise the backup retention period of the automated backups to 2 years, and then delete the DB instance.
options.why: The retention period can be set [between 0 and 35 days](../facts/rds.md#rds-backup-retention-range), so automated backups cannot reach 2 years.

options.text: Stop the DB instance instead of deleting it, and start the DB instance again when an auditor asks for the data.
options.why: A DB instance can stay stopped for [7 consecutive days](../facts/rds.md#rds-stop-max-seven-days); after that, RDS starts it again automatically.
options.misconception: a stopped DB instance stays stopped until someone starts it

explanation: Snapshots that you take, a final snapshot included, are independent of the DB instance: [Manual snapshots are not deleted](../facts/rds.md#rds-delete-instance-automated-backups-deleted) with it. They are [kept until you explicitly delete them](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-snapshots-user-initiated-kept-until-deleted), so the final snapshot holds today's data for the 2 years.
takeaway: To keep data after you delete a DB instance, take a final snapshot, which stays until you delete it.
twin: If the stem said "restore any second of the last week" instead: a point-in-time restore before the deletion, because RDS can recover to [any point in time](../facts/rds.md#rds-automated-backup-pitr-in-retention) in the retention period.
say: I'd take a final snapshot when I delete it; snapshots stay until we delete them.

stem: A company's web application stores its data in a Single-AZ Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The company wants to fix a performance problem without any change to the application's SQL queries. Dashboard read queries keep the CPU use near 90 percent at peak, but the number of database connections stays low. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Dashboard read queries keep the CPU use near 90 percent
the number of database connections stays low

options.text: Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance, and change the application's connection settings to use the proxy endpoint.
options.why: The proxy can [pool and share database connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-definition-pool-share), but connections are not the problem here, and each read query still runs on the DB instance.

options.text: Create a read replica of the DB instance, and change the application's connection settings to send its read-only queries to the replica.
options.why: Clients get [read-only access to the replica](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-async-read-only), which is enough for dashboards, and the read work moves off the primary.

options.text: Move the database to PostgreSQL on Amazon EC2 instances, and run a connection pooler and streaming read replicas that the team manages.
options.why: Self-managed replicas can take the reads, but on EC2 the team owns [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) of the database.
options.misconception: builds read scaling by hand when RDS read replicas exist

options.text: Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, so that the standby instance also serves part of the query load.
options.why: The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance [doesn't serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), so the CPU load on the primary stays the same.

explanation: The load comes from read queries, and the connections are few. A read replica is a [read-only copy of a DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-definition), made for [read-heavy database workloads](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-definition). The dashboards send their queries to the replica endpoint, and the primary keeps its CPU for the rest of the application.
takeaway: High read CPU with few connections points to a read replica, not to RDS Proxy or Multi-AZ.
twin: If the stem said "During spiky traffic, thousands of short-lived AWS Lambda invocations open connections, and the database returns too many connections errors at low CPU use" instead: RDS Proxy, because it pools [frequent short database connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-lambda-connection-pooling).
say: The reads are the load, so I'd move the dashboard queries to a read replica.

stem: A company runs an encrypted Multi-AZ Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in the us-east-1 Region. A customer managed AWS KMS key in us-east-1 encrypts the DB instance. A new contract requires cross-Region disaster recovery. If us-east-1 becomes unavailable, the company must run the database in us-west-2 from a copy with a recovery point of minutes, not hours. The copy must stay encrypted at rest. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: a recovery point of minutes, not hours

options.text: Rely on the Multi-AZ standby, because RDS fails over to the standby automatically if us-east-1 becomes unavailable.
options.why: RDS places the standby in [a different Availability Zone of the same Region](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-standby-same-region), so the standby is lost together with us-east-1.

options.text: Create a cross-Region read replica of the DB instance in us-west-2, and promote the replica if us-east-1 becomes unavailable.
options.why: A DB instance that [replicates asynchronously to a standby DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-region-async-replica-survives-region) in another Region keeps a copy there, and a replica [can be manually promoted](../facts/rds.md#rds-compare-failover-vs-promote).

options.text: Run MySQL on an Amazon EC2 instance in us-west-2, and manage binary log replication from the DB instance to it.
options.why: It can work, but the team then owns [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) and the replication itself.
options.misconception: builds cross-Region replication by hand when RDS has a managed replica

options.text: Choose a KMS key in us-west-2 to encrypt the read replica when the company creates the replica in us-west-2.
options.why: An encrypted replica in another Region needs a key there, so you [specify a KMS key in the destination Region](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-kms-regional-replica).

options.text: Use the ARN of the KMS key in us-east-1 for the read replica, so that both Regions use one key.
options.why: [KMS keys are specific to the AWS Region](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-kms-regional-replica) where they are created, so the us-east-1 key cannot encrypt the replica.

explanation: Multi-AZ protects against [DB instance failure and Availability Zone disruption](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-protects-az-disruption), not against the loss of a Region. A cross-Region read replica is the managed copy in us-west-2. Because the source is encrypted, the company chooses a [KMS key in the destination AWS Region](../facts/rds.md#rds-cross-region-replica-encrypted-source-dest-key) for the replica.
takeaway: Region-level recovery needs a cross-Region read replica, encrypted with a KMS key in the destination Region.
twin: If the stem said "if one Availability Zone fails" instead: the existing Multi-AZ deployment is enough, because it gives [automatic failover to standby](../facts/rds.md#rds-compare-failover-vs-promote).
say: Multi-AZ stays in one Region, so I'd add a cross-Region read replica with a KMS key in us-west-2.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for two steps that together give recovery in another Region with the LEAST operational overhead.

I mark the constraints: an encrypted Multi-AZ DB instance in us-east-1, recovery in us-west-2 if us-east-1 becomes unavailable, a recovery point of minutes, and encryption at rest with a customer managed KMS key.
Before I look at the options, I predict that the Multi-AZ standby already covers this, because RDS fails over to the standby automatically.

I remove the MySQL database on an EC2 instance, because the team would run the database and the replication by hand. I remove the KMS key ARN from us-east-1, because KMS keys are specific to the Region where they are created.

Between the Multi-AZ standby and the cross-Region read replica the difference is the Region. My first idea breaks because the standby is in a different Availability Zone of the same Region, so the standby is lost together with us-east-1. The replica in us-west-2 replicates asynchronously, so its copy is minutes behind, and a replica can be promoted by hand. It needs a KMS key in us-west-2.
Check: the cross-Region read replica and the KMS key in us-west-2 meet every constraint, and nothing extra runs on EC2. Time: 90 seconds.

stem: A company is choosing a database engine for a new application on Amazon RDS. The company's reporting team needs a read replica of the production database. On the replica, the team must create its own indexes and summary tables with DDL statements, and the replica must keep receiving all changes from the source DB instance. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
keywords: create its own indexes and summary tables with DDL statements
keep receiving all changes from the source DB instance

options.text: Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, create a read replica, and make the replica writable for the reporting team's DDL statements.
options.why: AWS does not allow an RDS for PostgreSQL read replica [to be made writable](../facts/rds.md#rds-replica-postgresql-not-writable), so the DDL statements fail.

options.text: Use a Multi-AZ DB cluster of Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, and run the DDL statements through the reader endpoint of the cluster.
options.why: The reader instances behind the reader endpoint [support only read operations](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-cluster-writer-reader-endpoints), so DDL statements there fail.
options.misconception: the readable standbys of a Multi-AZ DB cluster also accept writes

options.text: Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, and build a job that copies every change from the DB instance into a separate reporting DB instance.
options.why: A custom copy job works, but developers write, test and run the job, which a writable MySQL replica makes unnecessary.
options.misconception: writes replication code when the engine has a writable replica

options.text: Use Amazon RDS for MySQL, create a read replica, and set the read_only parameter of the replica to 0.
options.why: RDS for MySQL lets you [permit DDL SQL statements against a read replica](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-read-replica-mysql-ddl) through the read_only parameter, with no code to write.

explanation: The deciding need is DDL on a replica that keeps replicating. RDS for MariaDB and MySQL replicas use logical replication, and you can enable a MySQL [read replica to be writable](../facts/rds.md#rds-replica-mysql-logical-writable). After this parameter change on the replica, the team adds its indexes and tables there, and changes from the source keep arriving.
takeaway: DDL on a replica that keeps replicating points to RDS for MySQL or MariaDB, not to RDS for PostgreSQL.
twin: If the stem said "the team runs only SELECT queries on the replica" instead: either engine fits, because every read replica gives [read-only access to the replica](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-async-read-only).
say: A MySQL replica can take DDL with read_only set to zero; a PostgreSQL replica can't.

stem: A company runs an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance that is encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/rds. RDS takes a daily automated snapshot of the DB instance. A new policy requires that a separate backup account in the same AWS Region receives a copy of each day's backup that the backup account can restore. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/rds

options.text: Share the automated snapshot with the backup account directly, so that the backup account can copy it each day.
options.why: Sharing starts with [copying the automated snapshot](../facts/rds.md#rds-share-automated-copy-first) to a manual snapshot, because you can [share manual DB snapshots](../facts/rds.md#rds-snapshots-copy-both-share-manual) and not automated ones.

options.text: Copy the automated snapshot to a manual snapshot under a customer managed key, and allow the backup account to use the key.
options.why: The copy is made [using the customer managed key](../facts/rds.md#rds-share-default-kms-key-not-shareable), and the company can give the backup account access to that key.

options.text: Edit the key policy of the aws/rds key so that the backup account can use the key to decrypt the snapshot.
options.why: You [can't manage, rotate, or delete](../facts/rds.md#rds-kms-aws-managed-key-aws-rds) the aws/rds key, so its key policy stays under the control of AWS.

options.text: Each day, export the database with a dump tool from an Amazon EC2 instance, and upload the dump file to the backup account.
options.why: A daily dump can work, but the team builds, runs and tests the export and the restore, which snapshot copies do without code.
options.misconception: moves backups with scripts when snapshot copy and sharing do it

options.text: Share the manual snapshot copy with the backup account, so that the backup account can copy the snapshot and restore from it.
options.why: Sharing a manual snapshot [enables authorized AWS accounts to copy the snapshot](../facts/rds.md#rds-share-snapshot-copy-or-restore), and the backup account restores from its copy.

explanation: Two rules decide this. You can [share manual DB snapshots](../facts/rds.md#rds-snapshots-copy-both-share-manual) and not automated ones, and a snapshot [encrypted using the default KMS key](../facts/rds.md#rds-share-default-kms-key-not-shareable) cannot be shared. So the company copies the snapshot under a customer managed key, gives the backup account access to that key, and shares the copy.
takeaway: To share an encrypted automated snapshot, copy it under a customer managed key, then share the manual copy.
twin: If the stem said "the DB instance is unencrypted" instead: copy and share the snapshot with no key step, and the account can [directly restore a DB instance from the snapshot](../facts/rds.md#rds-share-snapshot-copy-or-restore).
say: I'd copy it to a manual snapshot under our own KMS key, then share the key and the copy.

stem: A company runs an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance on a general-purpose instance class. Every afternoon, queries slow down. Amazon CloudWatch shows moderate CPU use, low freeable memory, and read IOPS that are high and keep rising under load. The number of connections is steady and far below the limit. A short outage in the next maintenance window is acceptable. Which change is the MOST operationally efficient way to solve the problem?
keywords: read IOPS that are high and keep rising under load

options.text: Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance, so that the queries use pooled connections and need less memory.
options.why: The proxy can [pool and share database connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-definition-pool-share), but connections are steady here, and the queries still read the same data from storage.

options.text: Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, so that the standby takes part of the read load.
options.why: The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance [doesn't serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), so the reads stay on the primary.

options.text: Modify the DB instance to a memory-optimized instance class of a similar size during the next maintenance window.
options.why: A memory-optimized class holds more of the working set in memory, and [you can change your DB instance class](../facts/rds.md#rds-instance-class-changeable) in the maintenance window.

options.text: Add an Amazon ElastiCache cluster, and change the application code to cache the results of the most frequent queries.
options.why: A cache can lower the reads, but developers change the code and the team runs a cache cluster, which a class change avoids.
options.misconception: adds a cache and code changes when the database needs more memory

explanation: Low freeable memory and rising read IOPS mean that the working set no longer fits in memory. AWS advises enough RAM so that the working set [resides almost completely in memory](../facts/rds.md#rds-bp-working-set-in-memory). Memory-optimized classes such as db.z1d are [optimized for memory-intensive applications](../facts/rds.md#rds-class-memory-optimized-memory-intensive). The class change makes the database [temporarily unavailable](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-compute-scale-brief-outage) for a short time, which the stem accepts.
takeaway: Low freeable memory with rising read IOPS points to a memory-optimized instance class.
twin: If the stem said "the database returns too many connections errors at low CPU use" instead: RDS Proxy, because it keeps a [smaller number of long-lived connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-candidate-too-many-connections).
say: The working set no longer fits in memory, so I'd move to a memory-optimized class.
